entry.title: Three ways of not answering
entry.summary: I wasn't told, I cannot be made to say, and the question never got asked properly: three moves for the three ways of not answering.
entry.content:
Three moves, one idea. Unawares is I was not told. Plead the Fifth is I cannot be made to say. Depositioning is the question never got asked properly. They file in chapter III because they are the same character in three costumes, and because that chapter was the thinnest in the book and the one most in need of the vocabulary of the non-answer.

The Fifth is the entry to read carefully. The privilege is real, it is old, and the guide is not against it. The move is what the right becomes when it is the only sentence in the answer, offered in a hearing where what is at stake is a headline, not a cell.

Each carries a source: plausible deniability, the amendment itself, and Rule 30 on depositions. Each is also wired to the thing it answers. The subpoena now points at both moves that meet it, and the secret meeting at the move that hides inside it, because a reader who finds one half of a mechanism should be able to reach the other from the page.

Chapter III has the vocabulary it was missing. It is still the shortest chapter, and it is no longer the least useful.

entry.title: What a polish pass finds
entry.summary: Nothing structural, which is the interesting part. The shape of the guide was sound and the drift was in the sentences.
entry.content:
We walked every record against the contract, expecting to find broken entries and finding none. What the pass turned up instead was drift: three records written in a register the other 192 do not use, eight links that rendered nowhere, and three sightings that never named the thing they were sighting.

The voice problem is the one worth writing down. Crookmaxxing, JAQing Off and Bootcurious carried part-of-speech markers inside their senses, in italics, and a long explanatory clause where the book uses an epigram. The part of speech already has a field. The senses now open the way the rest of their kind opens, and Bootcurious stopped describing a person when it is filed as a condition that expires.

The dead links are the failure this guide is most likely to have. Eight records listed a term under both the related list and the confused-with pair. Both generators drop the twin from the related list, because the pair edge already renders it, so the link was authored, validated, and shown to nobody. A rule enforced in two places is a rule that eventually gets satisfied in neither.

The graph had drifted too. The transcript was named in the counter prose of Heckler's veto and Rally and was not wired to either, so the page told you to publish the transcript and did not offer you the entry that says how. Both edges are in now, and Rally no longer claims a habitat commits a fallacy it merely houses.

A polish pass is not a feature. It is the maintenance that keeps a field guide usable after a hundred small additions, and the finding is always the same: the entries are fine, the joins are where it rots.

The joins are also where the sibling tool starts. tresridge is the same discipline pointed at a .tres tree: it reads the families and the edges you already have, names what dangles and what nobody declared, and only then asks you to write the declaration. One gate in CI, exit 0 or 1, no prose to parse. The audit behind this post is the manual version: read the graph, find the references that go nowhere, fix them, make the fix a rule. tresridge is what that walk looks like when the tree is too large to walk.

entry.title: Three words that end an argument
entry.summary: The claim, the label, and the password: three species that use a word to close a question instead of answering it.
entry.content:
Three species arrived in one sitting and they share a job: a word that does the work of an argument. Ricochetoric fires a claim and lets the answer bounce off it. Ismatic is the label that ends the sentence before the sentence reaches the evidence. Shibbolether is the password that tells you which side of the line someone stands on.

What separates them is what the word is for. The ricochetoric wants you to answer the claim. The ismatic wants you to answer for the label. The shibbolether wants you to say the word. One is a projectile, one is a verdict, one is a test, and a reader who cannot tell them apart will use the wrong name on the wrong person, which is the failure this guide exists to prevent.

All three are filed in chapter II, beside the moves they borrow from, and each carries the tell that separates it from its nearest neighbour. The counters are the useful part: ask for the claim behind the label, ask who is testing whom, and answer the projectile with the question it was avoiding.

entry.title: A second sighting
entry.summary: Seven fallacies went into the reference end, and every fallacy already there got a second entry wired to it.
entry.content:
The seven are Kafka trap, Bulverism, McNamara fallacy, Nirvana fallacy, base rate fallacy, appeal to force, the fallacy fallacy. The same pass went back over the ones already filed and gave each a second sighting, a second entry that commits it in the wild.

The rule that forced the sweep: a fallacy filed on one sighting cannot be told apart from the habit of the entry that produced it. Two sightings is the smallest evidence that a move is portable, and a guide that keeps the rule can be checked from outside, because the graph either has the second edge or it does not. Every fallacy now carries at least two, so a reader can walk from the fallacy to the things that commit it instead of taking the entry's word for the pattern.

Three of the seven are the same trick at different distances. The Kafka trap makes the denial into the evidence. Bulverism answers the argument by explaining the arguer. The fallacy fallacy takes one bad argument as proof that the claim is false. All three end the argument without touching it.

The other four are about what gets weighed. McNamara counts what can be counted and files the rest as commentary. Nirvana compares a proposal to nothing and the present arrangement to nothing, so only the proposal looks expensive. The base rate fallacy weighs one vivid instance against the frequency it came from. Appeal to force prices the dissent before the merits are weighed at all.

A guide is only as good as its sightings. Two is the smallest number that is not an anecdote.

entry.title: Chapter VI answers the creatures
entry.summary: Five chapters name the failures. The sixth names the people who catch them, and the procedures that need no office at all.
entry.content:
A field guide that starts prescribing becomes a pamphlet, so the first five chapters only diagnose: name the creature, the move, the habitat, and stop there. Chapter VI breaks that rule on purpose. It is the first chapter whose entries are the answer rather than the description of the problem.

The keystones are offices. The clerk keeps the body's memory, the agenda, the roll call, the motions as adopted rather than as proposed. The poll worker runs the count everyone else argues about afterwards. The archivist keeps what nobody has asked for yet. The librarian holds the shelf the feed cannot sort. The caseworker reads the file. The editor decides what a sentence is allowed to mean. The moderator holds the line the heckler's veto is built to cross. The auditor follows the fee. Eight of them, each filed with a tell and a counter like any creature, because an office is exactly as easy to hollow out as a person.

The remedies are the ones available to somebody with no office at all: records request, lateral reading, the second source, the steelman, the transcript, the written reason, the public count, random draw, fee shift, sunset clause, the audit. Each is written as an instruction rather than a description. Read one out loud and you can run it tomorrow.

The split is the argument. A remedy without an office is advice. An office without a remedy is a title. Filing both in one chapter lets the guide say what a body needs and who is supposed to be holding it, and lets a reader see the gap when the answer is nobody.

Five chapters describe how a body loses the thread. This one describes the people who keep the receipts.
